back: Wind, solar, tidal, wave, geothermal, biomass and hydroelectric — they come from a natural supply that is continuously replaced.
Coal, oil, gas and nuclear — available in limited amounts and often extracted from the earth.
Advantages: little impact on the environment; reliable when windy. Disadvantages: visual pollution, expensive to install, can harm birds.
Advantages: clean and free once set up; works even on cloudy days. Disadvantages: expensive set-up, depends on sunshine, panels take space, storage is difficult and expensive.
Advantages: around 80% efficient; generates power for about 10 hours a day. Disadvantages: expensive to set up; can damage coastlines and harm marine life.
Uses 'hot spots' where molten rock near the earth's crust heats water. Very high cost, risks triggering earthquakes and limited to specific locations.
Advantages: renewable, fairly predictable, no fuel costs. Disadvantages: expensive, storm damage, affects marine life and shipping, only some coastlines suit it.
Water stored behind a dam flows through turbines. Reliable and quick to start; pumped storage can store energy. But very expensive and flooding valleys destroys habitats and homes.
A hydroelectric scheme that stores energy by pumping water back uphill, then releasing it through turbines when demand rises.
Organic material (wood, crops, food and animal waste) burned or turned into biofuel. Renewable if replanted, but releases CO₂ and smoke, needs land and can cause deforestation.
Advantages: large, reliable output and no CO₂ while generating. Disadvantages: radioactive waste stored for thousands of years, risk of serious accidents, very expensive to build and decommission.
Burning releases CO₂ (global warming) and sulphur dioxide (acid rain); they are finite and will run out; extraction damages landscapes.
The UK has committed to net zero emissions by 2050, including more offshore wind and cutting carbon emissions.
From 2030 the sale of new petrol and diesel cars is banned in the UK; some new hybrids can still be sold until 2035.
Convert free sunlight into electricity as a power supply or trickle charger — used in calculators, garden lights and solar chargers.
Uses mechanical movement, e.g. turning a handle, to generate and store energy without batteries — as in a wind-up torch.
Disposable (e.g. alkaline): cheap and convenient but create waste and contain harmful chemicals. Rechargeable (e.g. lithium-ion, NiMH): cost more at first but reused hundreds of times.
